name: Arthur Miller
bio: Arthur Miller, the playwright, was cited for contempt of Congress in 1956 (the House voted 373–9) after he refused, as a matter of conscience, to name people present at meetings of Communist writers he had attended years earlier. He had just been granted a passport and married Marilyn Monroe; his conviction was later overturned on appeal.
charges: Contempt of Congress — for refusing to name names before HUAC
convicted: Cited for contempt 1956; prosecution referred to the Justice Department
sentence: Faced up to a year and a $1,000 fine

name: Otto Nathan
bio: Dr. Otto Nathan was an economist and the executor of Albert Einstein's estate, cited for contempt of Congress in 1956 after refusing, on First Amendment grounds, to answer the House Un-American Activities Committee's questions about his beliefs and to surrender his passport.
charges: Contempt of Congress — for refusing to answer HUAC and to surrender his passport
convicted: Cited for contempt 1956; prosecution referred to the Justice Department
sentence: Faced up to a year and a $1,000 fine

name: Pete Seeger
bio: Pete Seeger, the folk singer, was cited for contempt of Congress in 1956 after refusing — on First Amendment grounds rather than the Fifth — to tell the House Un-American Activities Committee about his associations; he described himself to the committee as a 'banjo picker.' He was convicted in 1961 and the conviction was overturned in 1962.
charges: Contempt of Congress — for refusing to answer HUAC
convicted: Cited for contempt 1956; prosecution referred to the Justice Department
sentence: Faced up to a year and a $1,000 fine

name: Elliott Sullivan
bio: Elliott Sullivan, a New York actor, was cited for contempt of Congress in 1956 after refusing to tell the House Un-American Activities Committee of his past or present associations.
charges: Contempt of Congress — for refusing to answer HUAC
convicted: Cited for contempt 1956; prosecution referred to the Justice Department
sentence: Faced up to a year and a $1,000 fine

name: George Tyne
bio: George Tyne, a New York actor, was cited for contempt of Congress in 1956 after refusing to tell the House Un-American Activities Committee of his associations.
charges: Contempt of Congress — for refusing to answer HUAC
convicted: Cited for contempt 1956; prosecution referred to the Justice Department
sentence: Faced up to a year and a $1,000 fine

name: John T. Watkins
bio: John T. Watkins was a United Auto Workers organizer who admitted his own past cooperation with the Communist Party but refused, as a matter of principle, to name others before the House Un-American Activities Committee. Convicted of contempt of Congress, his appeal became the landmark 1957 Supreme Court decision Watkins v. United States.
charges: Contempt of Congress — for refusing to name former Communists
convicted: Convicted; reinstated on rehearing; appealing to the Supreme Court
sentence: One year and a $500 fine (under appeal)

name: John T. Gojack
bio: John T. Gojack was a vice-president of the United Electrical Workers and head of its District 9, convicted of contempt of Congress in May 1956 for refusing, on First Amendment grounds, to answer HUAC's questions about his associations. His conviction was later reversed by the Supreme Court (Gojack v. United States).
charges: Contempt of Congress — for refusing to answer HUAC
convicted: Convicted May 1956; on appeal
sentence: Faced up to a year and a $1,000 fine

name: Saul Grossman
affiliation: Michigan Committee for Protection of Foreign Born
bio: Saul Grossman was the executive secretary of the Michigan Committee for Protection of the Foreign Born, convicted of contempt of Congress for refusing to turn over his organization's records to the House Un-American Activities Committee in 1952. The U.S. Court of Appeals reversed his conviction in January 1956.
charges: Contempt of Congress — for refusing to surrender organization records to HUAC
convicted: Convicted; reversed by the Court of Appeals January 1956

name: Lee Lorch
bio: Dr. Lee Lorch was a mathematician and anti-segregation activist — fired in turn from City College, Penn State and Fisk University for his civil-rights work — who was indicted for contempt of Congress after declining, on First Amendment grounds, to answer HUAC while teaching at Fisk. The Justice Department dropped the charges in April 1956, conceding the indictment should not have been returned.
charges: Contempt of Congress — for refusing to answer HUAC
convicted: Indicted; charges dropped by the Justice Department April 1956

name: Paul Robeson
bio: Paul Robeson — the Black singer, actor, and activist — was held in contempt by the House Un-American Activities Committee in June 1956 when, subpoenaed in its passport probe, he refused to say whether he was a Communist and turned the questioning back on the committee. He had been denied a passport for years because of his political views.
charges: Contempt of Congress — and denial of a passport for his political views
convicted: Held in contempt by HUAC June 1956

name: Bernard Deutch
bio: Bernard Deutch was a University of Pennsylvania student convicted of contempt of Congress for refusing, on First Amendment grounds, to name people he allegedly knew to be Communists during a 1954 appearance before the House Un-American Activities Committee.
charges: Contempt of Congress — for refusing to name names before HUAC
convicted: Convicted of contempt of Congress
sentence: Convicted; faced jail and a fine

name: Herbert Simpson
bio: Herbert Simpson was one of three Portland, Oregon residents convicted of contempt of Congress for refusing to answer the Velde committee (HUAC) during its 1954 West Coast hearings. He was sentenced to ten months and a $250 fine and was appealing before the Ninth Circuit in 1956.
charges: Contempt of Congress — for refusing to answer HUAC
convicted: Convicted; on appeal (1956)

name: Don Wallam
bio: Don Wallam was one of three Portland, Oregon contempt-of-Congress defendants from the Velde committee's 1954 West Coast hearings, sentenced to a year and a $250 fine and appealing his conviction in 1956.
charges: Contempt of Congress — for refusing to answer HUAC
convicted: Convicted; on appeal (1956)

name: Alden Whitman
bio: Alden Whitman, a New York Times copy editor, was one of six people indicted for contempt of Congress in December 1956 for defying, on grounds other than the Fifth Amendment, the Senate Internal Security Subcommittee's 1955 inquisition into the New York press.
charges: Contempt of Congress — for defying the Senate Internal Security Subcommittee
convicted: Indicted December 1956

name: Robert Shelton
bio: Robert Shelton, a New York Times copy editor, was one of six indicted for contempt of Congress in December 1956 for refusing to cooperate with the Senate Internal Security Subcommittee's probe of the New York press.
charges: Contempt of Congress — for defying the Senate Internal Security Subcommittee
convicted: Indicted December 1956

name: Seymour Peck
bio: Seymour Peck, an editor on the New York Times Sunday magazine, was one of six indicted for contempt of Congress in December 1956 for defying the Senate Internal Security Subcommittee's inquisition into the press; he had admitted past Communist membership but refused to name associates.
charges: Contempt of Congress — for defying the Senate Internal Security Subcommittee
convicted: Indicted December 1956

name: William A. Price
bio: William A. Price was a New York Daily News reporter fired the day he refused to answer the Senate Internal Security Subcommittee's questions in its 1955 press probe; he was among the six indicted for contempt of Congress in December 1956.
charges: Contempt of Congress — for defying the Senate Internal Security Subcommittee
convicted: Indicted December 1956; also fired by his paper

name: Herman Liveright
bio: Herman Liveright was a former New Orleans television programmer (WDSU) cited and then indicted for contempt of Congress in 1956 for declining, on grounds other than the Fifth Amendment, to tell the Senate Internal Security Subcommittee whether he had ever been a Communist.
charges: Contempt of Congress — for defying the Senate Internal Security Subcommittee
convicted: Cited 1956; indicted December 1956

name: Mary Knowles
bio: Mary Knowles was a librarian employed by the Quaker Plymouth Monthly Meeting in Pennsylvania, indicted for contempt of Congress in December 1956 for refusing to answer a Congressional committee's questions about her associations. Her stand inspired the 1956 film 'Storm Center.'
charges: Contempt of Congress — for refusing to answer a Congressional committee
convicted: Cited; indicted December 1956

name: Pauline Feuer
bio: Pauline Feuer was a New Orleans educator cited for contempt of Congress in 1956 after telling the Senate Internal Security Subcommittee it had no authority to inquire into her personal beliefs.
charges: Contempt of Congress — for defying the Senate Internal Security Subcommittee
convicted: Contempt citation recommended to the Senate (1956)

name: Frank Wilkinson
affiliation: American Committee for Protection of Foreign Born
bio: Frank Wilkinson was a Los Angeles housing official turned civil-liberties organizer who, at the House Un-American Activities Committee's 1956 hearings, relied solely on the First Amendment in refusing to answer — exposing himself to a contempt citation. His resistance culminated in the Supreme Court case Wilkinson v. United States.
charges: Contempt of Congress — for refusing, on First Amendment grounds, to answer HUAC
convicted: Faced a contempt citation for his 1956 HUAC defiance
